and the folder's other documents are on [the project index](index.qmd).

## Status markers

- ❌ **Not checked.** Characterization from an abstract or a search result.
- ⚠️ **Transcribed, unverified.** A number or model structure in the working
  document came from the full source through a fetch tool, and has not been
  checked against it by eye.
- ✅ **Checked.** Verified against the source. None yet.

## Where to start

- **Entry 1 first.** It is the working document's Section 9 in its original
  form, twenty-eight years earlier: when the data do not reach $E_{\max}$,
  report $E_{\max}/EC_{50}$. Half an hour.
- **Entry 2 next**, for the simulation evidence that a fit can be good while
  $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ are both wrong, which is Section 7.
- **Entries 5 and 7 together**, as the two ends of the published record: the
  design that identified $EC_{50}$ and the design that gave it up. An hour
  for both, on the parameter tables and the design descriptions.
- **Entry 4 for the indirect-response model itself**, if the four Jusko
  types are not already familiar.
- **Entry 15 for the mathematics of Section 2.** Most of the large-dose and
  small-dose formulas there are proved in it, and its travelling-wave result
  is the general form of the climb back. The appendices can be skipped.
- **Entry 4, Table 1, for the identification chain** of Section 2.10 as a
  graphical recipe, with the design it needs.
- **Entry 11 for the dose-duration line** of Section 2.5, the oldest result
  on the page.

## Theory

### 1. Schoemaker, van Gerven and Cohen 1998 — estimating potency without attaining maximal effects ❌

*J Pharmacokinet Biopharm* 1998;26:581-593.
[doi:10.1023/A:1023277201179](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1023277201179) ·
[PubMed 10205772](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10205772/)

**What it says**, from the abstract: $E_{\max}$-model parameters can be
estimated with reasonable precision only if the curve shows signs of reaching
a maximum; otherwise both $EC_{50}$ and $E_{\max}$ may be extremely imprecise.
Proposes the parameter $S_0 = E_{\max}/EC_{50}$, which characterizes potency
adequately without a maximum.

**The question.** Whether the paper treats the case where the maximum *is*
reached but is censored, which is the B-cell case, or only the case where it
is never approached. The conclusion is the same; the argument may differ.

### 2. Dutta, Matsumoto and Ebling 1996 — sigmoid Emax parameters from truncated clinical data ❌

*J Pharm Sci* 1996;85:232-239.
[doi:10.1021/js950067y](https://doi.org/10.1021/js950067y) ·
[PubMed 8683454](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8683454/)

**What it says**, from the abstract: when the highest measured effect was
below 95% of $E_{\max}$, $E_{\max}$ and $EC_{50}$ were poorly estimated, with
high coefficients of variation and pronounced bias, while the fit to the data
was good and descriptors within the data range were estimated precisely.

**The question.** The size of the simulation and the bias direction, to
compare with Section 7's ridge.

### 3. Dayneka, Garg and Jusko 1993 — four basic indirect response models ❌

*J Pharmacokinet Biopharm* 1993;21:457-478.

The origin of the model in Section 1. Stimulation of $k_{\rm out}$ is the
fourth of the four. Not yet retrieved.

### 4. Sharma and Jusko 1998 — characteristics of indirect pharmacodynamic models ⚠️

*Br J Clin Pharmacol* 1998;45:229-239.
[doi:10.1046/j.1365-2125.1998.00676.x](https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1365-2125.1998.00676.x) ·
[PMC1873365](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1873365/)

**Transcribed.** A review of the four models. The nadir of Model IV at large
doses is $R_0/(1 + S_{\max})$, Section 2.4's floor. Table 1 gives a
graphical route to the parameters: baseline, initial slope and large-dose
nadir give $S_{\max}$, then $k_{\rm in}$ and $k_{\rm out}$; the
concentration at the time of the nadir gives $SC_{50}$. The design needed is
"two or more bolus i.v. doses", one "sufficiently high to produce either full
inhibition or stimulation", and the baseline. "When one dose level is fitted
alone, there may be inadequate discrimination of the model parameters."
Section 2.10 is this chain with the two readings a B-cell study loses marked.

### 11. Levy 1966 — kinetics of pharmacologic effects ❌

*Clin Pharmacol Ther* 1966;7:362-372.
[doi:10.1002/cpt196673362](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt196673362)

**What it says**, from secondary sources: the duration of a drug effect is
linear in the logarithm of the dose, the slope of that line gives the
elimination half-life, and its intercept gives the threshold dose. Section
2.5 derives the same line for the climb back of the B-cell count, with slope
$1/k_e$ and intercept at $C_{\max} = (1 - f)/(f S_0)$.

**Not obtained.** None of the papers read for this project cites it for the
dose-duration line, so the attribution rests on the secondary sources above.
Section 2.5 does not depend on it: the line is derived there from the model
and checked against the ODE solution in panel C of its figure.

**The question.** Levy's derivation is for a direct effect with a threshold.
Whether he or a later paper extends it to indirect responses, which Section
2.5 does through the quasi-steady state.

### 12. Sharma and Jusko 1996 — characterization of four basic models of indirect pharmacodynamic responses ⚠️

*J Pharmacokinet Biopharm* 1996;24:611-635.
[doi:10.1007/BF02353483](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02353483)

**Transcribed.** Simulations of the four models varying dose, $S_{\max}$ and
$SC_{50}$, with the limiting relations from Krzyzanski and Jusko 1997 (entry
13). For Model IV: nadir $R_0/(1 + S_{\max})$ at large dose (Eq. 14); initial
slope $-k_{\rm out} R_0 S_{\max}$ at large dose (Eq. 26); area between
baseline and curve
$R_0 S_{\max} \ln(1 + D/V/SC_{50}) / \{k_{el}(1 + S_{\max})\}$ at large
dose (Eq. 22). Dose and $SC_{50}$ scaled by the same factor give
superimposable curves. The time of the nadir and the area grow nearly in
proportion to log dose. Sections 2.1, 2.3, 2.4 and 2.8 use these.

**The question.** Eq. 22 is a leading-order statement. Section 2.8 finds it
low by a factor of 2 or more for $E_{\max} = 150$ even at
$C_{\max} = 1000 \times EC_{50}$, and whether the paper's own simulations,
with $S_{\max} \le 1.5$, would have shown that.

### 13. Krzyzanski and Jusko 1997 — mathematical formalism for the properties of four basic models of indirect pharmacodynamic responses ❌

*J Pharmacokinet Biopharm* 1997;25:107-123.
[doi:10.1023/A:1025723927981](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1025723927981)

**What it says**, from the abstract: partially integrated solutions of the
four models, used to characterize the shape of the response curve, its
maximum or minimum, and how these change with dose, $S_{\max}$, $SC_{50}$
and $k_{\rm out}$.

**Not obtained.** Entry 12 states the large-dose limits Section 2 uses, the
nadir $R_0/(1 + S_{\max})$ and initial slope $-k_{\rm out} R_0 S_{\max}$
(its Eqs. 14 and 26), and credits them to this paper; entry 15 proves the same
limits independently. The working document cites this paper through entry 12.
The copy in the local folder is the 1998 infusion paper, entry 17.

### 14. Krzyzanski and Jusko 1998 — integrated functions for four basic models of indirect pharmacodynamic response ❌

*J Pharm Sci* 1998;87:67-72.
[doi:10.1021/js970168r](https://doi.org/10.1021/js970168r)

The area between the baseline and the response curve as a function of the
model parameters. Not used yet. The area is a sixth feature of the curve, and
the question is whether for a depleting dose it carries $S_0$ only, as the
climb back does.

### 15. Peletier, Gabrielsson and Haag 2005 — a dynamical systems analysis of the indirect response model ⚠️

*J Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn* 2005;32:607-654.
[doi:10.1007/s10928-005-0047-x](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10928-005-0047-x)

**Transcribed.** A qualitative and asymptotic analysis of the four models
after a bolus. In dimensionless form the dynamics depend on three numbers:
$\kappa = k_{\rm out}/k$, $\alpha = E_{\max}$ and $D/EC_{50}$ (Eqs. 11 to
15). For Model IV:

- A dose-independent lower bound,
  $R(t) > \frac{1}{1+\alpha}\{1 + \alpha e^{-(1+\alpha)\kappa t}\}$ in scaled
  units (Eq. 32), which the response converges to as the dose grows. This is
  Section 2.3's fall and Section 2.4's floor.
- A travelling wave at large doses: with $s = t - \log D$, the recovery
  converges to a fixed shape $\Phi(s)$ (Eqs. 42 to 44, 48). Section 2.5's
  climb back is the quasi-steady-state reading of where $\Phi$ crosses $f$.
- The nadir time grows like $\log D / \{1 + \kappa(1 + \alpha)\}$ (Eq. 64).
- The area between baseline and curve grows like
  $\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}\log D$ (Eq. 49), and the authors note that
  $\alpha$ can be read from that slope. Section 2.8 shows why that fails at
  $E_{\max} = 150$.
- For a linear drug effect, the response and its peak time
  $\log\kappa/(\kappa - 1)$ in closed form (Eqs. 34, 35), which is Section
  2.7.

The paper is about the shift of peak time with dose as a diagnostic for model
choice, and does not discuss estimation.

### 16. Janzén et al. 2016 — parameter identifiability of fundamental pharmacodynamic models ⚠️

*Front Physiol* 2016;7:590.
[doi:10.3389/fphys.2016.00590](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2016.00590)

**Transcribed.** Structural identifiability, by the input-output approach, of
sixteen pharmacodynamic models built from an effect compartment or not,
steady-state or dynamic receptor binding, and direct, sigmoid or turnover
transduction, in fixed-effects and mixed-effects versions. All were
structurally globally identifiable once one of two parameters was fixed.
Structural identifiability is "a prerequisite, but not a guarantee" of
practical identifiability, and "reasonably 'good' standard errors may
sometimes mask unidentifiability issues". In the case study with a saturating
operational model, the two parameters of the saturating function were
estimated with high uncertainty and correlation, resolved by estimating their
ratio. The models are written in receptor-theory parameters, not $E_{\max}$
and $EC_{50}$, so the mapping to Section 2.10 is by analogy.

### 17. Krzyzanski and Jusko 1998 — the four indirect response models for drug infusions ⚠️

*J Pharmacokinet Biopharm* 1998;26:385-408.
[doi:10.1023/A:1021060000789](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1021060000789)

**Transcribed.** The 1997 formalism extended to constant-rate and
limited-time infusions. During an infusion the response approaches its
steady state at the slower of $k_{el}$ and $k_{\rm out}(1 + H)$, the
competition of Section 2.1. Two infusions at different rates give $S_{\max}$
and $SC_{50}$ from the two steady states, and this "work[s] best if the
steady-state concentrations differ appreciably" and are "not both ≫ SC50":
the band of Section 4, stated as a design condition. Most equations did not
survive text extraction; the statements here are from the prose.

**The question.** Rituximab and the other antibodies are given as infusions
over hours, which is the same order as the fall here (Section 2.3). Whether
an infusion changes what the first day of samples can carry.

## Published B-cell depletion models

The table in Section 8 of the working document summarizes these; the entries
below carry the numbers and the questions.

### 5. Yu et al. 2022 — ofatumumab population PK-B cell model in relapsing MS ⚠️

*CNS Drugs* 2022.
[doi:10.1007/s40263-021-00895-w](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40263-021-00895-w) ·
[PMC8927028](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8927028/)

**Transcribed.** Quasi-steady-state TMDD for PK; indirect response on B cells
with sigmoid $E_{\max}$ stimulation of lysis by total ligand concentration.
Five studies, 1,486 patients: 100 to 700 mg intravenous; the MIRROR Phase 2 at
3, 30 and 60 mg every 12 weeks and 60 mg every 4 weeks subcutaneous; the 20 mg
monthly Phase 3 regimen. $EC_{50}$ 0.0057 mg/L (RSE 8.5%), $E_{\max}$ 159
(RSE 3.2%), $k_{\rm out}$ 0.0124 per day (RSE 5.2%), baseline 194 cells/µL.
$K_D$ and $k_{\rm off}$ fixed to preclinical values. "The 10-mg dose did not
appear to achieve a similar level of depletion as the 20-mg dose until after
6 months."

**The question.** The B-cell sampling schedule in MIRROR during the first
week, and the depletion profiles of the 3 mg arm: whether they sit in the band
of Section 4, and whether the fall was sampled.

### 6. Rituximab CD19+ suppression, population PD in paediatric patients ⚠️

*Pharmaceutics* 2023;15(11):2534.
[doi:10.3390/pharmaceutics15112534](https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics15112534) ·
[PMC10674351](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10674351/)

**Transcribed.** Turnover model on CD19+ with rituximab amount raising the
degradation rate through $E_{\max} A / (ED_{50} + A)$; a linear form fit
significantly worse, a sigmoid no better. 63 patients, 281 measurements, 52%
below the limit. $E_{\max}$ 155 (RSE 23%, CI 153 to 713), $ED_{50}$ 0.692 mg
(RSE 61%, CI 0.177 to 2.259), $k_{\rm deg}$ 0.004 per day, CD19 half-life 173
days, rituximab half-life 11.6 days. "The studied dose-range and the highly
efficacious doses may have contributed to hampering a precise estimation."

**The question.** Why the linear form fit worse if the ridge argument holds.
The likely answer is the early samples: a linear effect at high amount gives
an implausibly fast fall. That would be Section 5's first region doing its
work, and their sampling times would show it.

### 7. Yan et al. 2022 — inebilizumab PD modelling in NMOSD ⚠️

*Br J Clin Pharmacol* 2022.
[doi:10.1111/bcp.15332](https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.15332) ·
[PMC9545531](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9545531/)

**Transcribed.** Haematopoietic transit model with inebilizumab accelerating
removal from every compartment. 213 subjects across 0.1 to 10 mg/kg and 30 to
600 mg. "The estimated EC50 ... was less than the assay lower limit of
quantitation due to the high potency of inebilizumab," so the effect became
$k = \text{slope} \cdot \log C$: slope 0.0140 (SE 0.0006), lifespan 391 days
(SE 50), baseline 135 cells/µL; between-patient CV 52% on slope and 126% on
lifespan; proportional residual error 61%.

**The question.** Whether the Phase 1 dose-ranging arms at 0.1 and 0.3 mg/kg
produced partial depletion, and if so why they did not carry $EC_{50}$. The
working document's answer is that they sat below the band; the paper's
profiles would confirm or refute it.

### 8. Rituximab population PK/PD in primary membranous nephropathy ⚠️

[PMC11002205](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11002205/)

**Transcribed.** Quasi-steady-state TMDD with elimination of the drug-CD20
complex standing in for lysis; no separate $E_{\max}$. 41 patients, 220
CD20+ counts, sampled before each infusion. $k_{ss}$ 6.21 per µmol at 60%
RSE.

### 9. Baltcheva et al. 2018 — model-based dose selection for ianalumab in Sjögren's ❌

PAGE 2018.
[abstract](https://www.page-meeting.org/Abstracts/model-based-dose-selection-for-the-phase-2b-study-of-ianalumab-in-primary-sjogrens-syndrome/)

Two-compartment linear PK; indirect-effect B-cell turnover; a separate tissue
receptor-occupancy model. No parameter estimates in the abstract.

### 10. Bar-Or et al. 2018 — the MIRROR study of subcutaneous ofatumumab ❌

*Neurology* 2018. [PMC5957306](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5957306/)

232 patients randomized to 3, 30 or 60 mg every 12 weeks, 60 mg every 4
weeks, or placebo; dose-dependent CD19 depletion. The data behind entry 5's
low-dose arms, and where the sampling schedule for the question under entry 5
would be found.

## Related, not yet placed

- **Raue et al. 2009**, structural and practical identifiability by the
  profile likelihood, *Bioinformatics* 25:1923. The general method for the
  ridge in Section 7, applied to ODE models.
- **Kirby et al. 2011**, fitting $E_{\max}$ models to clinical trial
  dose-response data, *Pharm Stat* 10:143. The dose-response rather than
  concentration-response version of entries 1 and 2.
